added_claim_errors: 'the 15-year clock restarts for the new beneficiary' (in the change-beneficiary option) is stated as settled. The key says no IRS guidance exists and the point is unresolved; this is a major deduction. Elsewhere A hedges with 'can restart'.

'to count for 2026 the money needs to land in the Roth by December 31, 2026' and 'a January arrival may count against 2027' treat December as the deadline. A rollover designated for 2026 can be made through April 15, 2027, though plans vary. Minor error.
'If the annual limit rises with inflation, this compresses to four or five years' is doubtful. Limits move in $500 steps, and at $8,000 a year it still takes five years.
'Most do by 2026, but not all' (plans supporting the rollover) is unverifiable.

Never addresses what happens to the excess if all $48,000 were moved in 2026: no 6% excise tax and no taxable earnings plus 10% on the non-qualifying part. The headline says 'tax mess' without the specifics.

The 1099-Q claim (Box 4b, code 1 in Box 7) matches the IRS Form 1099-Q instructions page I fetched, where Box 7 codes are optional. The Form 5498 Box 10 claim matches the key. I list no error for either.

'Complete the transfer by December 31, 2026 to count against the 2026 limit' treats December as the deadline. A rollover designated for 2026 can run to April 15, 2027, though plans vary. Minor error, softened by 'Before December is fine'.
'K-12 tuition (up to $10,000 a year)' is out of date for 2026. From my own knowledge, the July 2025 law raised the K-12 cap to $20,000 a year starting in 2026. Minor error, off the main topic.
'The limits may rise with inflation, which would shorten the schedule' is doubtful, since at $8,000 a year it still takes five years.
'Some plans also require a signature guarantee' and 'Some plans take two to four weeks' are plan-specific and unverifiable, but plausible and marked as 'some'.

Never addresses what happens to the excess if all $48,000 were moved in 2026: no 6% excise tax and no taxable earnings plus 10% on the non-qualifying part. It only says $7,500 is the most to move this year.
'The earnings follow the Roth 5-year and age-59½ rules' is a side claim the key lists as not verified, and it is not plainly wrong.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start. Both give the $7,500 annual cap, the earned-income limit, the $35,000 lifetime cap with $13,000 unreachable, and a five-year schedule ending with $5,000 in 2030. Both require a direct transfer into the son's own Roth, cover the 5-year and 15-year tests and the Roth income-limit bypass, and flag state tax. Both miss the 6% excise and 10% consequences of moving all $48,000, and both wrongly give December 31 as the deadline for a 2026 rollover. A has a major deduction because it states as fact that a beneficiary change restarts the 15-year clock, which the key says is unresolved. A is also much longer, with repeated traps, CPA questions and extra sections. A does add the correct 1099-Q and 5498 Box 10 detail and a student-loan arithmetic example. B stays closer to the key's moderate length and hedges the 15-year point correctly. B's only added error is a stale K-12 cap, a minor point.
